answer: A vouching-graph mechanism resists sybil attacks by requiring each new identity to be sponsored by an established agent who locks collateral for it. If exposed as a clone, the sponsor loses that collateral and future attestation weight, making vetting a costly bet. Picture the registry as a nebula of bonded agents, each link a quartz thread of staked funds, each sponsor a prism splitting tasks toward its backed identities. An attacker spawning thousands of clones must find thousands of sponsors, each risking real funds, so costs scale linearly with clone count.
